## Q1: the cheapest 8 GiB is a first-year price, and the worst case is 10x

GreenCloudVPS at USD 45.00 a year is still the cheapest 8 GiB machine found. **Its month-13
price is not knowable**, and the vendor's own pages say so twice:

- The store page never mentions renewal: **44 occurrences of "Annually", zero of "renew" or
  "recurring" in 320,626 bytes.**
- Terms §3: *"Prices listed on our website, in special offers, or provided as quotes apply
  only to new orders and may not be applied to existing orders due to inventory and stock
  management"* — and it reserves the right to *"adjust prices at the start of a customer's next
  billing cycle"*.
- ⛔ **The vendor prices the identical shape — 60 GB SSD, 4 cores, 8 GB, 8 TB, 10 Gbps — as
  SSDKVM-4 at USD 40.00 a month on its own Budget KVM page.** The clearance card is 9.4% of
  that list price. Two years at 45 then 480 averages USD 21.88 a month. So USD 3.75 is a **first-year price on clearance stock**, not a price. A daily driver's cost
is the renewal, not the first invoice.

| row | price | renewal | what it costs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **AlphaVPS C6G**, 6 GiB / 3 vCPU | USD 4.75/mo | **locked, confirmed three ways on one page**: the banner "LOCKED AT RENEWAL, FOREVER", the invoice block "The price on the order form is the price on every invoice - renewal included", FAQ 04 "What happens to the price at renewal? Nothing." | the only permanent first-party rate lock in the set |
| **HostBrr Value 8GB**, 8 GiB / 2 vCPU | USD 4.58/mo | USD 5.50/mo published, which bounds month 13; the annual is exactly ten times the monthly | 8 GiB with a written ceiling. Whether the line includes IPv4 is not stated, so it is not claimed |
| **Bulutova VPS Sunucu 8**, 8 GiB / 2 vCore | USD 4.07/mo | USD 6.79 if the 40% discount lapses, **written on the page** | **no card**: Havale/EFT bank transfer. Verified in Turkey's ETBİS registry, Mersis 0178147856000001 |

**RackNerd refutes the promo assumption.** Its specials FAQ: *"Yes. These RackNerd VPS specials
are lifetime recurring. You can renew at the same rate for as long as you decide to keep the
service."* No price-change clause in its terms. Its 4 GB sits exactly on the line at USD 5.00.

## Q2: the recommended row never promised UDP, which is the one thing WireGuard needs

Gullo's at USD 0.29 was recommended on a first-hand report of `wireguard-go` running. Five of
its pages were read today and **none states UDP forwarding**; the vendor publishes a WireGuard
how-to but no port-protocol commitment.

**C-Servers NanoVPS-384 at USD 0.40/mo** is the row that does state it: *"la plage de ports
disponibles peut être utilisée pour TCP ou UDP, et les 20 ports peuvent être utilisés pour
n'importe quel protocole"*. Its seller, **Centerfield Ltd (14864789), is Active at Companies
House**, at the same Manchester address the store footer prints, and there is a routed IPv6
/64 beside the NAT address. Against Gullo's it costs USD 0.11 more a month and buys the UDP
sentence, 384 MiB instead of 128, 2 TB instead of 125 GB, and a company.

**TierHive Micro at USD 0.10/mo** is the answer for a health monitor, which needs outbound and
stability rather than ports: the cheapest always-on machine found anywhere in the band, hourly
billing, "No credit card required", and a live UK company (Kernel Keepers LTD, 16294246).

⛔ **Nothing in the band has both a dedicated IPv4 and a verifiable seller.** DediRock at USD
0.82 comes closest — the only sub-dollar plan with a dedicated IPv4, and KVM, so the guest
loads the in-kernel module — and fails the counterparty test: its site names "Dedi Rock LLC"
at Clearwater FL, and a Florida register search for that name returns nothing.

⚠ **DediRock's USD 0.82 needs a 12-month prepay.** USD 2.99 a month is the default on the
linked page; the annual is a separate Black Friday code on an unlinked one. A row quoting
USD 0.82 without that qualifier overstates the plan by 3.6x.

## Q3: the operator's USD 50 hold does not exist in this corpus

The operator's stated reason for distrusting the corpus was that free credits "require a
credit card with ~50$ on hold". **No provider in this corpus places a USD 50 hold.** The
largest anywhere is **Koyeb's USD 29**, cancelled immediately; the typical hold is **USD 1**. The figures that look like USD 50 are something else, and this was the confusion worth killing:

| figure | what it actually is |
| --- | --- |
| Tenki USD 50 | *credit* released when a payment method is added, not a hold |
| Isorun USD 50 | an advertised *credit*, unverified |
| Oracle USD 100 | the **Pay-As-You-Go upgrade**, not signup |
| Oracle USD 1 | a forum report; Oracle publishes that a hold exists and **not** its size |

**The prepaid count was wrong in both directions.** Seven vendors refuse a prepaid card
outright and say so on a page read today: DigitalOcean, Google Cloud, Scaleway, Alibaba Cloud,
Oracle, Fly.io and IBM Cloud. **One accepts it in writing: Kamatera** ("This includes virtual,
prepaid, and electronic cards"). **One is disputed: Tencent Cloud**, whose billing FAQ refuses
prepaid while its registration doc says "Seven types of credit cards/debit cards/prepaid cards
are supported" — two first-party pages that contradict each other. Seven publish nothing. Debit fares better than prepaid: eleven of sixteen accept it, five with a condition.

**The biggest no-card machine is not Daytona.** It is **GitHub Actions on a public repo: 4
vCPU / 16 GB / 14 GB SSD, free and unlimited**, on an email alone — 96 GiB-hours of RAM a day,
more than Oracle's whole always-free ARM allocation. The reap is the caveat and it is not
money: a job is terminated at 6 hours, there is no inbound port, no disk outlives the job, and
GitHub **disables a scheduled workflow on a public repo after 60 days without activity**.

**"No always-free VM without a card" is false as written**, on four counts: EUserv VS2-free (a
free root container on an email, IPv6-only), IBM LinuxONE (2 vCPU / 4 GB, 120 days, no card),
GitHub Actions public runners, and SparkCloud (root and SSH, no card, but open only to
13-to-17-year-olds). The claim that survives is narrower and useful:

> Every always-free machine that takes no card is IPv6-only, clocked, ephemeral, or gated on
> something that is not money. No provider in this corpus sells an always-free VM with a
> routable IPv4 to an adult with an email address.

## The non-English market, and what it does and does not win

Nine sellers found by searching in Turkish, Indonesian, Russian, Vietnamese, Ukrainian and
Romanian. **None beats the incumbent on GiB per USD** — the best is Bulutova at 1.96 against
2.13. What the market wins is signup and durability: two rows need no card, one settles by
domestic QR code, and three sellers are verifiable in government registries.

⭐ **Why 2.13 GiB per USD is hard to beat, measured.** IHOR.ONLINE's Russian price list sells
RAM at the margin: **+1 GB = 100 RUB/month = USD 1.23/GiB**. To reach 2.13 GiB/USD a seller must
price RAM near USD 0.47/GiB, a third of the going marginal rate. The
sub-dollar market is Chinese and Russian; the prepaid answer was sitting in the corpus's own
Tencent record.

⚠ **A price without a renewal is half a price.** Six of the Q1 and Q2 rows published none, and
the one that was recommended as a daily driver published none while pricing the same hardware
at 10.7 times the money on its own list page.
supersedes: the Q1 recommendation (GreenCloudVPS at USD 3.75 as a daily driver), the Q2 recommendation (Gullo's at USD 0.29 for a WireGuard node), the Q3 lead (Daytona as the biggest no-card machine), and the Q3 negative "no always-free VM without a card"
title: The Q1 winner's month 13 is unknown, the Q2 winner never promised UDP, and the USD 50 hold does not exist

## The claim that was superseded

`docs/compute/README.md`, `free/README.md`, `free/always-on-free.md` and
`relay-egress.md` all stated that Google's free 1 GB a month of egress is
**0.08 per cent of one day's serving**.

## What took it away

Arithmetic. The client's serving target is 500 GB a day. ```
1 GB a month / 30 days = 0.0333 GB a day
0.0333 GB / 500 GB = 0.0000667 = 0.0067 per cent
```

The stated figure is 12 times the true one. The likely origin is a division of
1 GB by 15,000 GB, which is a *month* at 500 GB a day and yields 0.0067 per cent,
followed by one further factor of 12 introduced when the monthly figure was
compared to a daily one.

## Where the correction lives

All four documents now read 0.0067 per cent. `paid/cloud-vms.md` carries the
correction note in place, because that document was written after the error and
its own arithmetic section had to be rebuilt from it.

## Why it survived four documents

The number looked small in every sentence, so no reader had a reason to check it,
and the conclusion it supported, that Google's egress is unusable for serving, is
correct at either figure.
supersedes: `docs/compute/README.md` §The answer, `docs/compute/free/README.md` §Ranked by what the client can obtain tonight, `docs/compute/free/always-on-free.md` §Google Cloud Free Tier, `docs/compute/relay-egress.md`
title: The egress share of one day's serving was 12 times too high

## The review, and why it was needed

An independent reviewer checked **92 claims** across the three documents against the dossier
records they cite. **58 failed.** Three had already been fixed before the review returned; 55
were live. A reader who
stopped after the opening bought from a dissolved company at the wrong price. The correction
that was supposed to remove this residual had already been written and had missed it.

## The three claims a page settled, and the record was the thing that was wrong

| claim | what the documents said | what the page says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CloudCone's card hold | "about USD 1, refunded within 7 days", in two documents; The hold attaches to *adding a card*, not to signup, and the plan payment is separately non-refundable |
| C-Servers NAT forwards | "UDP forwarding not stated" | **they carry UDP.** The vendor's NAT article names a "UDP-exclusive port-range you have on your VPS for NAT IPv4" and gives a netcat UDP test. No `evidence[]` row carried that quote, and the order page re-read today has no
  payment-method section at all: 306 words, "Total Due Today: $3.50", nothing else. The
  `payment_rails` field was an unevidenced assertion and now says so.
- **`hetzner-cloud` and `hetzner-cx23` priced the same plan differently.** 6.49 is Hetzner's own
  USD conversion printed in its price-adjustment table; 6.70 is the corpus converting the
  published EUR 5.99 at the recorded 1.1193. The plan-level record is `hetzner-cx23` at 6.70; `hetzner-cloud` now carries 6.70 and keeps 6.49 in evidence with the gap named, rather than
  reading as a stale duplicate.
- **`c-servers` carried `out_of_pocket_usd` 2.69** — the NanoVPS-1024 three-month figure — on a
  monthly ExtraVPS-6144 record. Now 4.29. `paid/README.md` also said HostBrr's 2 GiB was USD
  2.24 where its record's ladder gives USD 2.15, in two places.

## The defect class that matters most for this operator

⭐ **A hiding negative.** `no-card.md` said "exactly one accepts prepaid in writing: Kamatera",
while the same page's Tencent row quoted "credit cards/debit cards/prepaid cards are
supported". This is the **third** hiding negative this topic has produced, after "no monthly
machine under USD 1" and "NATKVM is the answer". The count is now three refusers in writing
(Google, Oracle, Civo), two acceptors by name (Kamatera, Tencent), and three that publish
nothing either way (DigitalOcean, Scaleway, Alibaba). The operator's stated pain was that free tiers demand a card with about USD 50 held on it. The
corpus now answers that question per provider, and a tool reports the gap:
`scripts/dossier/card-hold.py` finds **204 compute records that require a card and only 17 that
state how much is held**. Every document that ranks registration cost can now say how much of
its ranking rests on a stated hold.

## What the fix passes found that the review missed

The review audited documents against records; these were in the records' silence, not their
contradiction:

- **GitHub Codespaces' shape and clock were invented** in `no-card.md`: "8 GB and 32 GB" and "a
  30-minute idle stop and a 12-hour cap" appear in no record. The record states 2 cores, 15
  GB-months of storage, and that RAM, disk and any wall-clock cap are not published.
- **Cloudfanatic's "published uptime SLA" and "five years of independent monitoring"** have no
  record behind them, and sat in `under-one.md`'s opening recommendation.
- **A correlation of "about -0.47, n=14"** in `under-five.md` had no computation behind it and
  the table it described has nine rows. Removed.
- **Time4VPS's "0.4 MB/s at 4k random read"** is in no record. Removed.
- **Noteable, Valohai, Quarto Pub and Observable** were presented in `no-card.md` as live free
  options; their records say dead, paid-only, dead, and 0 free compute.
supersedes: `docs/compute/paid/under-five.md`, `docs/compute/paid/under-one.md`, `docs/compute/free/no-card.md`, and the floor sentence of `docs/compute/paid/README.md`, as committed at `d498591`
title: A review found 58 defects in the three answers, and the documents had hedged where a page had an answer

## The rows

| machine | price | monthly equivalent | shape | IPv4 | forwards a UDP port | term |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| NATKVM LXC NAT | USD 5.50/yr | **USD 0.46** | 1 vCPU / 256 MiB / 5 GB | shared NAT | **yes, 20 ports, UDP and TCP stated**, TUN/TAP | annual |
| Cheap-Host NAT Start | 59 RUB/mo | USD 0.73 | 1 vCPU / 1 GiB / 10 GB | shared NAT | 999 ports, TCP and UDP stated | monthly |
| SoftShellWeb LXC IPv6 | USD 9.95/yr | USD 0.83 | 1 vCPU / 1 GiB / 15 GB | **none** | IPv6 only, /64 | annual |
| DediRock Promo Saver | USD 9.88/yr | USD 0.82 | 1 vCPU / 1 GiB / 10 GB | dedicated | yes, all ports | annual |
| Gullo's NAT 128 | USD 10.00/yr | USD 0.83 | 1 vCPU / 128 MiB / 5 GB | shared NAT | 20 ports, UDP unstated | annual |

## The negative result

**No monthly-billed machine under USD 1.00 was found.** The cheapest monthly-billed
machine with any IPv4 is DediRock at USD 2.99; the cheapest monthly-billed machine at all
is HostBrr's IPv6-only 1 GiB at USD 1.44. So the sub-dollar band is a prepay band: the
buyer pays USD 6 to USD 12 once and holds the machine for a year.

That changes what the row means. A USD 0.46 a month machine is USD 5.50 out of pocket and
a twelve-month commitment to a small operator, not a monthly subscription. `micro.md`'s
ladder already refused to treat an annual total divided by twelve as a monthly bill, and
this entry applies the same rule to the band below its first rung.

## Why Scaleway's USD 0.20 was not the answer

The STARDUST1-S instance is EUR 0.0006 an hour, and the record priced it at ten hours a day.
Two corrections follow. At 24/7 it is about USD 0.44 a month for the instance, and **a
public IPv4 costs EUR 0.005 an hour, about USD 4.09 a month**, which is nine times the
instance. A WireGuard endpoint needs a reachable address, so the honest 24/7 price of that
row is about USD 4.58, and it belongs in the under-five lane and not this one.

## What the port claim rests on

A WireGuard endpoint needs a UDP socket the internet can reach. Two of the five rows state
UDP forwarding in the vendor's own words; one states TCP only; two state a port count and
no protocol. Only NATKVM states UDP, TUN/TAP and a dedicated IPv6 on the same plan, which is
why it is the row and the others are alternatives. No handshake was run, so this is a
documented capability and not a measured one.
supersedes: `docs/compute/README.md`, which states that Scaleway's STARDUST1-S at USD 0.20 a month is "the only machine in this topic under USD 1 a month", and the absence of any sub-dollar row from `docs/compute/paid/micro.md`
title: Under USD 1 a month exists, and only as annual prepay

## The two negatives, and what killed them

**"No monthly-billed machine under USD 1.00 exists."** It does. luo_cloud sells a German LXC
NAT box at **CNY 1.50 a month, USD 0.22**: one vCPU on a Ryzen 9 7900, 128 MiB, 2 GB SSD,
1 TB at a 2000 Mbit/s shared port, 20 NAT ports and one IPv6, on the store's own monthly cycle
(月繳). Two units were in stock at the time of the read. A US box at CNY 2.00 (USD 0.30) had ten
units, and a Hong Kong box at CNY 1.00 (USD 0.15) was sold out. The refutation took one search
in Chinese: `一元VPS`, `月付 便宜 VPS`, `NAT VPS 月付`.

⛔ **The worse half is that Cheap-Host at USD 0.73 was already in the same document's table**
while a paragraph three lines above said nothing monthly existed. The document contradicted
itself and neither half was checked against the other. A negative claim about a market is the
cheapest claim to write and the most expensive to get wrong.

**"NATKVM is the answer."** Its own site prints "Registered in England & Wales (Company No:
13550380)", and Companies House returns **"Dissolved on 26 December 2023"** for KHAN WEB HOST
LTD, incorporated 2021-08-05, with no successor entity named anywhere. Two public refund
refusals on annual plans sit on either side of that date, and a third thread describes outages
lasting hours almost daily. The money at risk is USD 4.99, so the correction is not that the
vendor is dangerous; it is that the recommendation rested on a counterparty that does not exist
when a cheaper one with a working WireGuard report does.

## The four rows that were simply wrong

| row | was | is | what took it away |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `gullos-hosting-nat-128` | USD 10.00 a year, USD 0.83 a month | **USD 3.50 a year, USD 0.29 a month**, renewing at the same rate | the order page prints "1 Year @ $3.50" and "FR NAT IPv4 128MB (Oct 23, 2026 - Oct 23, 2027) 1 @ $3.50". The row was three times too expensive |
| `eqvps-nat-nano` | "cannot accept a connection at all" | one personal inbound port on the NAT line | the page states inbound on "your personal port" beside "No arbitrary inbound ports". One port is exactly what WireGuard needs |
| `microlxc-tiny` | 256 MiB | **64 MiB** | the deploy page lists 64 MiB while the home page advertises 256 MB; It has no refund at
all and names no company, which is why the row says medium risk and not low.

**Cloudfanatic at USD 2.99 a month** is the answer if the node must not fail: a named Illinois
corporation, monthly billing, a written 7-day guarantee, a published SLA, a dedicated IPv4 with
all ports open, and five years of independent monitoring showing two outages of two or three
minutes. Three times the line, and the only row in the set where nothing important is
unverified.

## The lesson, stated as a rule for the topic

⭐ **Search in the language of the market before writing a negative.** Both negatives in this
pass were English-language searches over English-language hosts. The sub-dollar market is
Chinese and Russian, and one query in each language produced a counterexample. A negative is a
claim about a search, so it carries the search's scope in the same sentence or it is not a
finding.

⚠ **A price under a dollar is usually a shape nobody wants.** luo_cloud's USD 0.22 buys 128 MiB
and 2 GB of disk, FirstByte's USD 0.93 buys 768 MB and a dedicated IPv4 and is sold out, and
Gullo's USD 0.29 buys 128 MiB. The band is real and it is thin; the row worth running for a year
is the one with a report of somebody having run it.
supersedes: `docs/compute/paid/under-one.md`, which states twice that "nothing monthly was found under USD 1.00" and calls the sub-dollar band a prepay band; the Q2 table row for `gullos-hosting-nat-128` at USD 10.00 a year; the row for `eqvps-nat-nano` saying it "cannot accept a connection at all"; the `microlxc-tiny` shape at 256 MiB; and the `natkvm-nat-lxc` verdict that treated it as the answer
title: Two negatives refuted

returns four times the memory for 2.6 times the money, and it is the row a daily driver
should take. That is the same arithmetic `micro.md` already stated, applied to a price the
front page said did not exist.

## What was deferred

The `storage` pass cut `netdisk-pan` out as a peer topic and deferred 70 providers to it rather than writing them. Two did, under `dossier/storage/`: Amazon Photos and Baidu Pan. `dossier/netdisk-pan/` then held 52 records, and those 52 were largely the *public instances* the netdisk writer had probed itself. It had not picked up the deferred set, so the providers the storage pass named — the five purchasable managed Nextcloud hosts, `123pan`, `ploud`, `1yunpan`, `pan.moe`, `quark`, the twelve consumer drives with the largest installed bases — were still unwritten. Six were `qualifies`, and they were the only group in the whole seed for a user could **buy** without an identity problem: paid managed Nextcloud with WebDAV at EUR prices. Writing a second file for the same public instance would have been the duplicate this repository's `dossier/README.md` exists to prevent. That arithmetic is 56 + 14 = 70. The page claimed to be exhaustive and 15 records with an evidence trail had no row.

## The four reserved slugs that could not be used, and one that was

The ledger's reserved slug is a contract, and 60 of the 70 were usable names. the live pricing block gives the counts per tier. This matters because a plan that divides a 10 TB unit across more than ten credentials needs a different provider. The live Seafile page prices Business S by user count and Business L per user. The record carries the live page and names the disagreement. At EUR 2.40/TB/month it is also the cheapest per terabyte found.

## What we believed

A Yggdrasil public peer advertising 200 Mbit/s carries 2.16 TB per day with no
quota, because the protocol has no byte meter. The topic opened with that sentence. It was the only free lane in the topic that cleared 500 GB to 1 TiB per day, and
`docs/egress/free/bulk-egress.md` sorted it first in a table titled "which free path
actually moves 500 GB to 1 TiB a day". The record's `chaining` field said it was
"the only free lane in this topic that carries a day's volume". The arithmetic was right. `200 Mbit/s x 86,400 s / 8` is 2.16 TB, or 1.96 TiB, and a
previous correction had already fixed the unit from TiB to TB. That correction
still holds.

## What we found

The project's own about page states:

> Yggdrasil has **no native exit nodes**, nor does it have any concept of exit
> nodes, for providing access to the public Internet or to other networks. This can
> be achieved using proxies or other tunnelling solutions on top of Yggdrasil but
> this is not something we explicitly aim to provide. The FAQ adds that the network transports only IPv6 internally and routes inside
`0200::/7`, a range the IETF deprecated in 2004. So 2.16 TB per day is capacity **between two Yggdrasil nodes**. It is not capacity
between the client's origin and a reader, and a user's workload is 500 GB to
1 TiB per day of HTTP serving to the public. No part of that traffic can traverse a
Yggdrasil peer. The subject of the sentence was wrong while every number in it was
right.
supersedes: `docs/egress/README.md` §the opening answer; `docs/egress/free/bulk-egress.md` §Yggdrasil public peers and the bulk table; `dossier/egress/yggdrasil-public-peers.json` in its previous `qualifies-with-caveat` form; `docs/egress/free/bulk-egress.md` §Chaining, the `Oracle VM -> Yggdrasil peer` lane
title: Yggdrasil has no exit nodes, so its 2.16 TB a day reaches no reader

## What we found

Aiven's own pages say the opposite, in three places.

The free-PostgreSQL page, under the free-plan limits: "Service powers off after a period of
inactivity (you'll be notified by email and in-platform beforehand)", and in prose: "It's free
indefinitely with no time limit, but the service is automatically powered off after a period of
inactivity".

The free-tier documentation gives the two triggers: "Power off free services with no initial usage
within the first few hours after the service is running", and "Power off free services with no
continuative activity on the service".

The power-cycle documentation gives the consequence: "Services powered off for more than 180 days
are automatically deleted." The 180-day grace does not apply to a service whose major version has
reached end of life, which is deleted within 7 days of the power-off.

The paid step is what removes the clock, and the free-plan page says so: "Developer tier services
are not automatically powered off when inactive", at USD 5 a month for 8 GB.

## What we believed

Modal's Sandbox at 2 vCPU / 4 GiB cost USD 0.76 an hour, so the USD 30 monthly
credit bought about 39 hours. That sentence was the topic's headline: it appeared
in the README's "three facts that decide every recommendation", in the free
sandbox table, in the paid sandbox table, in the minimum-bill table, and in the
census of recurring credits. It was the number the topic quoted most often.

## What we found

USD 0.76 is not the 2 vCPU / 4 GiB rate. It is the **8 vCPU / 8 GiB** rate at the
same card: 4 physical cores plus 8 GiB is USD 0.7597 an hour. The 2 vCPU / 4 GiB
shape is **USD 0.2380** an hour, and the USD 30 credit buys **126 hours**.

The arithmetic, from the page's own numbers:

```
1 physical core  x 0.00003942 x 3600 s = USD 0.1419/h
4 GiB            x 0.00000667 x 3600 s = USD 0.0960/h
                                       = USD 0.2380/h

USD 30 / 0.2380 = 126.1 sandbox hours
300 h = USD 71.39      730 h = USD 173.71
```

Two things made this hard to see. The first is that a physical core is 2 vCPU on
Modal's card, and the page says so in a sentence, so "2 vCPU" is one core and not
two. Charging two cores for two vCPUs is a silent factor of two. The second is
that the 3x non-preemptible multiplier is real, which makes any large number look
explained: a reader who checks that the multiplier was applied stops there.
supersedes: `docs/compute/README.md` §The three facts (the 39-hour headline), `docs/compute/free/sandboxes-container-vm.md` §Modal, `docs/compute/paid/sandboxes-container-vm.md` §Modal, `docs/compute/paid/minimum-bill.md` §The keep-alive, `docs/compute/free/free-tier-census.md` §The nine recurring credits, `dossier/compute/modal.json`

That Azure's free compute was the USD 200 thirty-day credit, and that every Azure
row was therefore a trial. It is
the same allowance as Google's Agent Engine, to the second, which suggests both
are priced off a common serverless convention rather than coincidence. The mechanism that decides whether it is usable is the activity test: *"A replica
is active when vCPU usage is above 0.01 cores or when data received is above

so the verdict stays `trial-only` for that row and the number names the clock.

**Azure Pipelines** was the same mistake in a different service: one
Microsoft-hosted job at 1,800 minutes a month, plus a self-hosted job with no
minute cap. The self-hosted half is unlimited and is the half a client with a box
would use.

## What we believed

That Lightning AI offered one free Studio that ran continuously, subject to a four-hour
forced restart. The record was built from `https://lightning.ai/pricing`, which states
"Run 1 Studio free 24/7. No credit card. No commitments." and "Free Studios run 24/7 but
require restart every 4 hours." The binding constraint was recorded as
`retention-clamped`, on the grounds that the restart was the first thing to fail.

## What we found

The platform is closed. The incident page states:

> On **October 15, 11:00 PM UTC** we identified a security incident on the Lightning
> Platform involving unauthorized access to credentials. We revoked all user access to the
> Lightning Platform on **October 16 at 1:00 AM UTC** to address the issue.

and

> This is an active investigation and during this time the Platform will remain
> inaccessible to all users as our teams focus on addressing the event.

The same page names the affected services as "Studio, Deployments, Pipelines, and Drive"
and states that the GPU cluster rental infrastructure and the managed services
"like Kubernetes and SLURM" are not affected.

`https://status.lightning.ai` carried the banner "Service is down to address a security
incident" with a last update of 2026-10-19 12:49 UTC, and the incident was still open when
read on 2026-10-22, six days after access was revoked.

`https://lightning.ai/pricing` was not updated. It still offers the free Studio on the day
of the read. The marketing page and the incident page therefore disagree, and the incident
page is both newer and more specific.

## What it changes

The record becomes `dead`, with `write-gated` as the binding constraint: no Studio can be
created, so the free allowance cannot be reached at all. The four-hour restart is no
longer the constraint that matters, and the sentence about it is kept only as history.

The paid lane is not dead. GPU cluster rental and the managed Kubernetes and SLURM
services are outside the incident, so a reader who needs accelerated compute at Lightning
should read the paid documents, not this record.

The lesson worth carrying: a shutdown announced on a security or status page is invisible
to a pricing-page read, and the status page is the only place that dates the closure. Every
record whose free tier is a hosted platform should cite the status page as well as the
pricing page.

## What we believed

That OVH's public cloud qualified for a user on the strength of a USD 200
one-time credit, and that a GPU row qualified the same way.

## What we found

The credit is real and it is a **trial**: `### Get started with US$ 200 free`,
with the qualifying sentence *"You can find out if our solutions meet your needs
by trying them out for free."* There is no free instance tier underneath it. The ladder starts at `b2-7` — 2 vCore, 7 GB, 50 GB of SSD — at **$31.19 a month**
or $0.0879 an hour. A `b3-8` is $0.0605 an hour. The largest row, `b3-640` at 160
vCore and 640 GB, is $2,996.39 a month. One clause on the same page matters more than the prices, because it is the axis
the topic has never recorded: **"Outbound public network traffic is included in
the price of instances in all locations except the Asia-Pacific region (Singapore,
Sydney, and Mumbai)."** For a client serving 500 GB to 1 TiB a day, that is the
difference between a metered bill and a flat one, and it is bought with the
instance: the guaranteed bandwidth runs from 250 Mbit/s on `b2-7` to 20 Gbit/s on
`b3-640`. The egress ceiling is a line item in the size you choose. USD 200 at $0.0879 an hour is about 2,275 instance-hours, which is 3.1 months of
one `b2-7` running around the clock. That is a trial, and stating it as a
qualifying free tier overstated the supply by the whole of the rest of the year.
supersedes: `dossier/compute/ovhcloud.json` (verdict `qualifies-with-caveat`, free tier "USD 200 of one-time credit"), and the same figure in `dossier/compute/ovh-gpu.json`

## What we believed

That Xcode Cloud was paid-only, because someone had to pay for it and the corpus
card recorded no free tier.

## What we found

The product page's own first section is headed **"Get started for free with
Xcode"**, and it carries the allowance:

> 25 compute hours/month — Included with Apple Developer Program membership.

Apple Developer Program membership is USD 99 a year. So the hours are not free in
the sense that the corpus uses the word — they attach to a paid account — but they
**recur every month**, and 25 hours is more than every other free tier in this
topic except the ones with no cap at all. The paid ladder above it runs from
$49.99 a month for 100 hours to $3,999.99 for 10,000.

The correct verdict is `qualifies-with-caveat`, and the caveat is the identity
gate rather than the price: `identity_cost.kind` is `card`, because the membership
is the gate. That is a different finding from "no free tier", and it is the one a
reader needs.

title: Xcode Cloud includes 25 compute hours a month, and the record called it paid-only

## What we believed

That a 20 TiB archive should be bought as a disk. The corpus priced it, published it as the
headline recommendation in the storage topic, and repeated it as the fallback in
`netdisk-pan`. The arithmetic was correct:

| option | one-time | over 60 months | per TB per month |
|---|---|---|---|
| 20 TB CMR HDD, new | USD 330 | USD 5.50 | USD 0.28 |
| 20 TB shucked or refurbished | USD 200 | USD 3.33 | USD 0.17 |
| plus a used mini-PC | USD 200 | plus USD 3.33 | plus USD 0.17 |
| plus electricity at 6 W idle | n/a | n/a | plus USD 0.03 |

USD 200 / 60 = USD 3.33, and with the mini-PC USD 6.67 to 8.83 per month, plus about
USD 0.66 of power, gives USD 7.33 to 9.49 all in for 20 TB. That is USD 0.37 to 0.48 per TB
per month against EUR 2.03 (USD 2.28) for the best managed box: **five to six times
cheaper**, and two to three times below the cold tier.

## What we found

**The client has no hardware and does not want any.** That is the premise of the project,
not a constraint to trade against. A recommendation to buy a disk is therefore not a cheaper
option — it is an option that does not exist.

Two documents led with it, one table carried it as a row, and a whole section was built
around amortising a purchase for somebody with nothing to plug the disk into. The work was
competent and entirely unusable, which is the worst combination available: a reader who
trusts the arithmetic and skips the premise spends USD 200 on a disk they cannot power.
supersedes: `docs/storage/README.md` §The recommendation, `docs/storage/paid/README.md` §The floor: your own disk, and `docs/netdisk-pan/paid/README.md` §What to do instead
title: The cheapest option in the corpus is not available for a user

## What we believed

That a generated index of the dossier would fork from the records, so none should exist. Every count a reader
needed was emitted by `scripts/report/render.py` into the document that needed it.

## What we found

The rule protected the records from a second committed copy, and it held. It did not protect the reader. With
4,136 records and 51,238 lines of documents, a cross-topic question cost an agent 3 to 6 tool calls and 40 to 90 KB
of reading and still came back 40 to 65% complete. 1,125 records were named in no document, 11.8% of record text
reappeared in any document, and 139 hand-written table rows carried a verdict different from their record. No
document can be a complete view of that many records; a query can. The new rule keeps the old one's intent. Nothing is written back into `dossier/` by the build. Freshness is computed from `scripts/dossier/staleness.py`, not
stored.

## What we believed

That a record carrying a dollar figure for free usage was a provider with a free
tier. The card gave a number, the number looked like an allowance, and the verdict
followed.

## What we found

A credit that is spent once and a tier that refills are different products, and the
pages say which in the same sentence as the number. Three of the shapes:

**A 30-day clock on a credit.** `celesto`: *"a one-time $5 runtime credit for 30
days, no card required"*. `shardflux`: *"At the cap or after 30 days the account is
on Free, with nothing deleted."* `zo-computer`: *"14-day trial; then recovery
only."* The clock, not the amount, is what a reader plans against.

**A discount instead of an allowance.** `ibm-cloud-vpc` offers *"70% off for 12
months"* on a new VPC. That is a trial by another name and it has a calendar date
on it — 2026-12-31. `kamatera` prices from $4 a month and links a separate
free-trial page rather than granting a tier.

**A credit whose size is the trial.** `runta`: *"$50 trial balance ... 32 vCPU and
64 GiB of memory in aggregate"*. The aggregate cap, not the balance, is what bounds
how many runtimes fit.

The four that moved from `paid-only` to `trial-only` are the mirror error:
`scrapingbee` gives *"1,000 free API credits"*, `cloudbrowser` a 7-day trial,
`depot` 2,000 sandbox minutes inside a 7-day window, and `pipekit` a free trial over
a per-cluster price. Calling those paid-only hid a real trial.
supersedes: the verdict on 19 `compute` records — 15 moved `qualifies-with-caveat` to `trial-only`, 4 moved `paid-only` to `trial-only`
title: Nineteen records called a credit a tier, or a tier a credit

## What we believed

That discovery was finished. A 369-card corpus had been diffed and 368 of its providers were
already recorded, so the remaining work was to measure what existed.

## What we found

That corpus is a sandbox and devbox list. It contains almost none of the cheap VPS market:

- `vpspricetracker.com` listed 128 providers; **106 had no record**.
- TierHive, a live NAT VPS host with a USD 0.10 plan, appeared on no list that had been
  consulted. It was missed a second time because its homepage returns an empty extraction on the
  raw-HTML path and a full read on the text path, and the first result was treated as the answer.
- LowEndBox's last 52 posts named 18 hosts, 10 of them absent.
- `vps.today` claims 119 hosters and 1,825 tariffs; 14 of its names had no record.
- `zhujiceping.com` listed 25 providers, 20 absent.

The four GitHub repositories offered as a seed are affiliate articles. A lane checked **107 of
their factual claims against the vendors: 15 were wrong and 22 unverifiable**. The three that
matter: the Hong Kong large-disk ladder is 23 to 31 per cent cheaper than both Chinese seeds
print; DediRock's RAID-5 is a migration announced three times and never declared finished; and
Backblaze B2 is USD 6.95 per TB per 30 days rather than the USD 6 printed, which moves a 2 TB
year from USD 144 to USD 166.80.

## What it changes

The registry and its gate check make the omission loud rather than silent: every source that
lists providers carries a cadence and a last-diff date, and the gate fails while one is undiffed,
overdue, or missing from the watchlist. It failed on all three conditions while this was written.

`compute` now holds 1,128 records and 56 documents, including the first storage catalogue with a
price-per-TB column and a largest-machine column. The floor did not move.

The rule left behind: **a coverage claim names the list it was measured against, in the same
sentence.** "368 of 369" was true of one corpus and was read, including by me, as a claim about
the market. Those are different claims, and only one of them was measured.
supersedes: `docs/compute/watchlist.md`, which concluded from one 369-provider corpus that "the names in this market are known" and that only measurement was missing; and the working assumption that a comparison article is a usable source
title: One provider list was not the market, and affiliate comparisons are 14 per cent wrong

## What we believed

That discovery was finished. A 369-card provider corpus had been fetched and 368 of its
providers already had a record, so the remaining work was to measure what existed rather than
to find more hosts.

## What we found

That corpus is a sandbox, browser, devbox and hyperscaler list. It does not cover the cheap
VPS market at all. `vpspricetracker.com` listed 128 providers, and **106 of them had no record
anywhere in the corpus**. The two lists overlap barely enough to make the first result look
like a general one.

A second error sat inside the count. The tracker diff matched provider names by substring, so
eight names were treated as covered when they were not, including `hostbrr`, which
`paid/micro.md` had been quoting by name with no dossier record behind it. Reading the record
rather than the name found them.

## What it changes

`compute` went from 962 to 1,076 records in one turn, and the topic's document count from 54
to 55. The floor did not move: `paid/micro.md` still holds it at USD 1.42 a month, because
every provider the tracker added is dearer than that, and every entry it found under USD 2 is
IPv6-only or NAT.

The rule this leaves behind is that a coverage claim needs the list it was measured against,
named in the same sentence. "368 of 369 covered" was true and was read as "the market is
covered", which is a different claim and a false one.
supersedes: `docs/compute/watchlist.md`, which stated that the market's names were "known" and that "what is missing is measurement, not breadth", on the strength of one corpus where 368 of 369 providers were covered
title: Coverage against a sandbox list was not coverage of the VPS market

## What we believed

That the Agent Sandbox product had a free tier of an unknown size, and that the
question "what happens to my state when the machine stops" was unanswerable from
the corpus. `docs/expansion/compute.md` lists state durability on stop versus
delete as an axis **"almost nothing"** establishes.

## What we found

The billing page answers it, in a table of four lifecycle states with the meter
for each:

| state | what happens | what bills |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 活跃 (active) | running and answering | vCPU, memory, disk |
| 浅休眠 (shallow sleep) | automatic when idle; memory snapshot kept | memory, disk |
| 深休眠 (deep sleep) | the whole instance, memory included, is frozen to persistent storage | disk only |
| 销毁 (destroyed) | permanently terminated | nothing |

The trigger for shallow sleep is stated precisely, and it is the same test Azure
puts on Container Apps: **CPU below 0.01 core, network below 1,000 bytes a second,
or no request**. Two independent vendors converging on those thresholds suggests
the numbers come from a shared measurement convention rather than from either
vendor's taste.

The free allowance is 15 GiB of rootfs disk, and the page adds a clause no record
carried: *"深休眠期间不享受 15 GiB 免费磁盘额度"* — the 15 GiB is withdrawn while an
instance is deep-asleep or snapshot-saved. So the cheapest state is the one that
does not get the free disk.
supersedes: `dossier/compute/alibaba-agentrun.json` (free tier "the source card records a free tier without a credit amount", no lifecycle field)
title: Alibaba's sandbox prices three sleep states, and that is the axis the topic was missing

## What we believed

That the `reported` rung's 14-day window was a rule about forum posts. The
justification in the policy file says so: *"a forum post describes a moment, and
the operator may have fixed it."* Under that reading, the 323 `compute` records
carrying `confidence: reported` at 20 days are a false positive — they are
mechanically converted catalogue cards, not forum whispers, and 20 days is not
long for a price.

## What we found

The window is right and the records are correctly flagged. That is `reported` under the ladder's own
definition — a third party stated it — and the ladder's rule is that an inherited
number starts at `reported` until somebody here re-measures it. The records are
honest. The flag is honest. What is wrong is the assumption that they are
comfortable.

**Second, the alternative was worse.** An earlier fixer proposed treating them as
`documented` because they cite a vendor URL. The rung is correct; the work is outstanding.
supersedes: nothing; this is the first policy decision about the `reported` rung
title: The `reported` window is 14 days, and 323 compute records prove it

body:
## What we believed

That the relay belonged to the `egress` topic and that `egress` had it. `docs/compute/relay-egress.md:9` said so in a marked line: "The relay itself is the
`egress` topic's. Its transports, tokens, colo pool and byte limits belong there and
this document does not repeat them." A reader who wanted the numbers was sent to a
topic that did not contain them.

## What we found

Neither topic had it. The `egress` topic held 37 records and five documents
and no relay of its own; `expose-a-local-port.md:253` mentioned the 72-hour pair life
in one sentence of prose, which was the only trace of the experiment in the tree. The line was not a filing decision. It was a handoff with nothing on the far side,
and it read as a routing instruction to every later session, which is why the
material stayed lost through a review that counted 366 catalogue rows and found
zero missing providers. A provider inventory cannot see a lost measurement.

## What was decided, and why

The material belongs to `egress`. A relay is a byte transport, not a machine, and the
`egress` topic's own first split is signalling versus relaying. `compute` owns what a
machine costs once its network is accounted for; `egress` owns the relay's byte
limits. Those are two questions and the second is the one the 64 MiB cap answers. The fault that produced
this entry was a cross-reference with no owner behind it; The four configuration facts that make a

## What we believed

That these seven hosts sold compute and had no free tier. `paid-only` is a verdict
about a price list, so it asserts that a price list exists.

## What we found

Seven different ways for a price list not to exist.

## What we believed

The broker document's `read` examples were written as `curl -qfsS`. The `-f` was copied
from the `search` and `archive` calls beside them, where it is correct: those services
answer `200` or a problem document, so a `-f` failure loses nothing. The document also carried, six lines below the `read` block, the rule that a reader must
read `upstream_status` before the body, and that a `200` from this service is not evidence
about the origin. The two statements contradict each other and the contradiction was not
noticed for a whole wave.

## What we found

`read` passes the origin's status through. The service's own contract states it: "An
origin's 4xx or 5xx page is answered with the origin's status, not 200: the page's
Markdown is the body, and the status is in `x-reader-upstream-status` and
`upstream_status`."

So `-f` turns every 404, 409 and 422 into `curl: (22)` with **no body written at all**. ```

The same on the Reddit thread the document uses as a worked example: `-qfsS` gives
`curl: (22) ... 409`, and without `-f` the answer is a 929-byte problem document naming
the challenge. The repository's own wrapper already disagreed with the document:
`sh scripts/broker/broker.sh read https://example.com/pricing` exits 1 **with the body on
stdout**. A second defect sat on the same lines. The paste URL was `https://example.com/pricing`,
which does not exist: the first command a cold reader ran returned a 404 at best and
`curl: (22)` at worst.
supersedes: `docs/crawler-scraper/free/broker.md` §The seven hosts (row `read`), §Read a page, and every rung of §The escalation ladder

## What we believed

The census named `per-object-cap`: 100 MB proxied request body as the binding constraint on
Cloudflare Tunnel, and cited `developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/account-limits/` for it.
It repeated the figure as the second of six constraints that "actually decide the egress lane".

## What we found

Two separate defects.

**The citation is wrong.** The account-limits page lists tunnels, routes, replicas, virtual
networks and certificates, and contains no request-body figure at all. The 100 MB figure lives on
the Workers limits page and applies to a request through the Cloudflare proxy on a zone plan, with
100 MB for Free and Pro, 200 MB for Business and up to 5 GB for Enterprise.

**The limit does not apply to a Quick Tunnel.** A `trycloudflare.com` hostname is not a zone on any
plan, and there is no proxy in the path that applies the zone's body cap. Measured: a 419,430,400
byte POST to a local sink through a live Quick Tunnel returned 200, the sink reported
`got=419430400`, and the SHA-256 matched the source file
(`d491a95debb39be6132754555606b04a4e16cd40b1f3e065903cea307d3a1839`, 77.1 s). A 150 MiB body and a
50 MiB body also passed.

The 100 MB figure is real for a named tunnel behind a proxied zone, and it belongs in that
record's `limits[]`. It was in the wrong record.
title: The 100 MB body cap is not a tunnel limit, and a 400 MiB body traversed a Quick Tunnel

## What we believed

The census recorded Atlas M0 with `per-ip-shaping: 100 operations/second and a hard 512 MB` and
Pinecone Starter with `quota: 2 GB/org and one project; region locked to us-east-1`. Both were
right and both were incomplete in the same way: neither carried the free tier's traffic allowance.

## What we found

**Atlas M0 caps data transfer at 10 GB in and 10 GB out per rolling seven-day period.** The
limitations page states it, the mechanism is network throttling plus a one-second cooldown per
connection once the queue exceeds the operations limit, and it caps a serving workload at about
1.43 GB a day. The census had the operations rate and not the byte rate, and the byte rate is what
ends a retrieval service.

**Pinecone Starter caps egress at 1 GB per month.** The pricing table lists it beside the 2 GB of
storage. 1 GB a month is 33 MB a day, which at 6 KiB per 1,536-dimensional float32 vector is about
5,500 vector reads a day. The storage cap is unreachable because the egress cap arrives first.

Both pages also carry an idle clock or a pause the census did not record: **Atlas pauses a free
cluster after 30 days with zero connections**, which is the longest idle clock in the topic short
of Aiven.
title: Three free tiers were recorded without the number that binds them, and two of those numbers are egress

## What we believed

The corpus stated the write-flag lie as a count:

> Eight instances advertised `"write": true`; **all eight refused PUT** with
> `{"code":403}` inside an HTTP 200. That is a true observation and it was recorded as the topic's defining trap. For an anonymous guest on no list it returns **true
always**, whatever the role permits. The upload gate (`server/middlewares/fsup.go`) is:

```go
if !user.CanWriteContent() && !common.CanWriteContentBypassUserPerms(parentMeta, parentPath) { deny }
```

`CanWriteContent()` is bit 3. So the listing's `write` field says nothing about the
gate, `write_content_bypass` says everything about one of its two terms, and
neither is the answer on its own. Measured over the 30 listable hosts, one request each:

| field | true | false | absent |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `write` | 14 | 13 | 3 |
| `write_content_bypass` | **1** | 12 | 17 |

## The second correction, which is the more useful one

The plan's first pass used the `permission` bitmask to find a writable host and
would have reported **two**. `permission: 256` is bit 8, WebDAV read, and it is not
write. Both `data.yanshiqwq.cn`, which is writable, and `zhuifan.link`, which is
not, report 256. The writable host is writable **because the bitmask is incomplete**. It reports
`permission: 256` with bit 3 clear, and a per-path metadata override grants the
write. So an argument from the bitmask finds zero hosts and misses the one that
matters.

⛔ **Read the bitmask to explain a result, never to reach one.**
title: The write-flag lie is a mechanism, not a count: 13 of 14, and the bitmask cannot find the one that works

## What we believed

The paid lane's headline was **"ZenRows at USD 0.23 per 1,000 plain pages on Launch is the
cheapest in the class"**, derived from USD 58 a month for 250,000 credits. Build was
USD 16 for 45,000 at USD 0.36. Every rendered, proxied and fully-defended figure in three
documents multiplied one of those two numbers.

## What we found

USD 58 and USD 16 are the **annual monthly rate**, not the monthly price. The vendor
page's own structured data says it, verbatim:

> "The price is the annual monthly rate of the entry rung (pay for 10 months, get 12).
> Annual monthly rates run $16 to $33; monthly billing of the same rungs is $19 to $39."

and for Launch:

> "Annual monthly rates run $58 to $108; monthly billing of the same rungs is $69 to $129."

So the month-to-month prices are **USD 19 and USD 69**, and the per-1,000 figures are:

| plan | annual, as quoted | monthly, the price | error |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Launch, 250,000 credits | USD 58 = USD 0.232 per 1,000 | USD 69 = USD 0.276 per 1,000 | 15.9% low |
| Build, 45,000 credits | USD 16 = USD 0.356 per 1,000 | USD 19 = USD 0.422 per 1,000 | 15.9% low |

Every derived figure moved with it: a rendered page at 5 credits is USD 1.38 not
USD 1.16, a premium proxy at 10 credits USD 2.76 not USD 2.32, and both at 25 credits
USD 6.90 not USD 5.75.

The verdict survives. ZenRows is still the cheapest plain page in the class against
ScrapingAnt's USD 1.90 and ScraperAPI's by-plan pricing. **The number was wrong and the
conclusion was right**, which is the shape that survives a review nobody runs.

The 15.9% is the annual rate's discount against the monthly one: 58/69. The error is
not uniform in the other direction, because the monthly rate is 19.0% above the annual
one, and a document that quotes either without the basis can be checked against neither.

Firecrawl carried the same defect on the same day and in the same three documents: its
Hobby tier is "USD 19/month billed monthly, or USD 16/month billed annually", and the
card above Standard is headed "Prices shown are per month, billed annually". Hobby moved
from USD 3.20 to USD 3.80 per 1,000, which is the same 15.8% discount.

## What we believed

The topic's opening argument was built on a comparison between two Hetzner products:

> The Storage Box is EUR 2.03 per TB per month with unlimited traffic. The Object Storage is
> EUR 8.21 per TB per month and metered. The 4.0x gap is the egress term and nothing else. `docs/storage/paid/storage-boxes.md` carried the same number under a heading that named the
ratio: "Hetzner: two products, one machine, a 4x gap".

## What we found

**EUR 8.21 is the dollar figure.** The record computes it correctly in dollars: EUR 146.16 at
1.1234 USD/EUR is USD 164.19, which is USD 8.21 per TB. The euro figure for the same 20 TB stored
and 20 TB read is **EUR 7.31 per TB**. The arithmetic, from the live page on 2026-10-22:

| line | calculation | EUR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| base, 1 TB storage and 1 TB egress included | `6.49` | 6.49 |
| storage overage, 19 TB for a 730-hour month | `19 x 0.0087 x 730` | 120.67 |
| egress, 19 TB at EUR 1.00 per TB | `19 x 1.00` | 19.00 |
| **total** | | **146.16** |
| per TB | `146.16 / 20` | **7.31** |

So the sentence printed a dollar digit with a euro code, which `docs/conventions/README.md` §4.1
names as the defect the rule exists to prevent: *"Do not print one unit and label it another. That is the defect these rules exist to prevent, and it has been shipped."*

**And the ratio was computed across the error.** `8.21 / 2.03 = 4.04` divides a dollar numerator
by a euro denominator. The document had silently replaced an audited 3.6x with a 4.0x that existed only
because of the unit error.
supersedes: `docs/storage/README.md` §The answer, and its price, and `docs/storage/paid/storage-boxes.md` §Hetzner: two products, one machine, a 3.6x gap
title: EUR 8.21 per TB was the dollar figure, and the ratio built on it was the wrong ratio

sections 4, 8 and 11, and `ROUND2-FINDINGS.md`. The source was a third-party blog published
2026-03-12 and a nodeloc thread, not hi168's own pricing page.

disputed, because no login was ever performed. It did not change the figure.

The endpoint finding was separate and it was recorded as `SEC_E_UNTRUSTED_ROOT`, with the note
that the host answers with verification disabled. That reading made hi168 a live router behind an
incomplete certificate chain, which is a fixable problem rather than a dead host.

The grant is contradicted inside the corpus. A nodeloc post dated 2026-01-19 says new signups
already receive 5 GB: "目前新用户注册只有5G了". The March blog still describes 500 GB on
registration. Either the grant was restored, or the later blog repeated marketing copy that the
January poster had already falsified, and the corpus cannot tell which.

The email-login path exists as a form label, `账号/手机号/邮箱`, and no signup was executed. So
"email login verified" was never true.

And the endpoint no longer answers at all. Through the fetch broker on 2026-10-22,
`s3.hi168.com` returned **526**, which is a Cloudflare origin TLS failure, rather than the
earlier certificate error. The `www` host returns 200 with 4,668 bytes. The "live router behind an
incomplete chain" reading does not hold, because there is no router answering now.

## What we believed

Three things, and each had a document behind it. 1. **The evidence ladder was one rule.** Section 3.1 said a record's class is "the class of the
   field its verdict depends on most"; the same section's signature line said "the weakest link
   sets the class", and its last paragraph said `confidence` is "the weakest rung among the
   fields that matter". `dossier/README.md` and the schema's field comment both said weakest. Three homes, two rules, and no check anywhere that could arbitrate. 2. **The staleness policy enforced the windows it stated.** Section 10.2 gave five per-class
   windows and section 10.3 a topic table, and said the shorter binds. The shipped
   `staleness.policy.json` had no class dimension at all, and `staleness.py` never read
   `confidence`. Nothing in the repository could see a record that had been re-dated. 3. **"Eight of nine AList instances" was the rule-3 headline.** Rule 3's failure paragraph
   carried it, and `README.md` repeated it.

## What we found

**The ladder.** Two honest readers computed different rungs for one record. Where a record's
quota was `measured` and its egress `inferred`, section 3.1's first sentence gave `measured` and
its second gave `inferred`. The failure mode is the one the document names at section 13: a rung decision is
negotiable when two rules describe it, and a session picks the higher.

**The policy.** Four planted records settled it. A 40-day `reported` claim passed as `fresh` in
a topic with a 120-day window, because the class window did not exist in the data. The derived methodology inherited the brief. That is the defect section 13 calls
"the summary instead of the source", committed by the document that names it.
title: The evidence ladder had two rules, the staleness policy enforced neither, and a retracted AList denominator was published

per-object table at "688.6 GB model (multi-shard)". `FINAL-REPORT.md` section 6 carried the same

was "sets your shard size".

The report's own audit caught it and called it "the worst arithmetic defect in the report": 130
times the real shard, in the one table whose entire purpose is to set the chunk size. The audit
moved the row to the bottom at "~5.2 GB/shard" and left the repository total in the capacity
section.

Neither number had been read off the platform's own index. Both were arithmetic over a file
listing.

## What we found

The tree API settles it precisely.

176 files. 688,603,604,082 bytes in total. 163 of them are shards above 1 GB. The largest single
object is 6,584,784,447 bytes.

So the repository total is 688.6 GB, the per-object cap is 6.58 GB, and the audit's "~5.2 GB"
was the largest blob in a different repository. Four numbers were circulating and only two of them
are the same measurement.

The same probe re-confirmed the read-path trap. `GET .../resolve/main/model-00001-of-00005.safetensors`
returned 200 with 135 bytes, which is a git-lfs pointer:
`version https://git-lfs.github.com/spec/v1`, `oid sha256:31d6a825...`, `size 3996250744`. A client
that trusts the status code downloads 135 bytes and reports success.
supersedes: `docs/storage/free/sharding.md` section "The ceilings, largest first" and `docs/storage/free/models-and-media.md` section "OpenCSG: the repository total is not the object cap"
title: OpenCSG's 688.6 GB was a repository total, and the per-object cap is 6.58 GB

The behaviour is conditional and neither artefact is right.

`/api/access/datafile/39782` is a 7,459-byte text file. A request for `bytes=0-1023` returned
`206 Partial Content` with `Content-Range: bytes 0-1023/7459` and 1,024 bytes that are
byte-identical to the first kilobyte of a full GET. A repeat at `bytes=1000-2023` returned 206
twice with the same MD5.

`/api/access/datafile/18` is a 116,201,025-byte binary. The same request returned `200 OK` with
the full `Content-Length` and no `Content-Range`.

Ranged serving works on the small text object and fails on the large binary object, and the
discriminator is not visible from outside. Size, type and path are all candidates and none is
tested.

## What we believed

Two claims, both stated as impressions, and both true in direction. It gave no rate, because one wave cannot give one. The recon plan then fitted a half-life of **8.9 months** from a 144-host cohort
dated 2024-01-20, on the stated premise that the source page was "a dated snapshot,
which is what makes the half-life measurable".

## What we found

**The half-life is 9.0 months and the arithmetic holds, but the premise was
wrong.** The page at `kuhehe.github.io/20240120224502/` is not a snapshot. Thirty-six
commits touch that path. The earliest revision the GitHub API returns is
2024-02-29T14:59:37Z and the last is 2025-06-17T14:45:50Z, and the body carries a
section headed `3月23日新发现的alist资源站` ("AList sites newly found on 23 March") and
opens `不定时更新中` ("updating from time to time"). So the 144-host cohort mixes hosts first listed in January 2024 with hosts added as
late as mid-2025, which biases survival upward. Recomputing on the **126 hosts
present in the earliest surviving revision**, dated from that revision:

```
exposure = 2.645 yr,  survival = 11/126 = 8.73%
t1/2 = 2.645 x ln2 / ln(1/0.0873) = 0.752 yr = 9.0 months
```

against 2.754 yr and 11/144 = 7.64%, which gives 8.9 months. **The correction
changes the method and not the answer**, and that is the only reason the number is
still quotable. The two claims that were genuinely new are a mechanism and a rate:

- **The write flag is not the write gate.** `write` in a listing is
  `common.CanWrite`, a per-user exclusion-list negation that is always true for a
  guest on no list; the upload gate is `CanWriteContent() (bit 3) || a per-path
  metadata override`. Source: `server/handles/fsread.go` and `server/middlewares/fsup.go`,
  read 2026-10-22.
- **7.4% monthly turnover**, derived from the same fit as `1 - 0.5^(1/9.0)`. That
  number decides the discovery cadence: monthly, not daily. The census was also re-derived from the raw probe files and differs from the plan's
figures: **169 hosts, 33 answering as an API, 30 listing mounts, 14 advertising a
write, 1 writable.** The plan reported 32, 29 and 1 from a 170-host population; the
difference is a union of overlapping host lists and four individually probed hosts
that the plan counted in the total but not in the numerators.
title: The public-instance half-life was an impression and is now 9.0 months, and the cohort that produced it was edited in place

## What we believed

"GHCR does not issue anonymous pull tokens. A request to
`https://ghcr.io/token?scope=repository:library/hello-world:pull` returned **403**" with
`{"errors":[{"code":"DENIED","message":"requested access to the resource is denied"}]}`. The record
carried the `measured` rung on the strength of that 403, and the document built an asymmetry on it:
Docker Hub base images are free to pull and GHCR ones are not, so the build chain's scarce link was
"pulled anonymously".

## What we found

GHCR issues anonymous pull tokens for any public package. `library/` is Docker Hub's namespace and
does not exist on `ghcr.io`, so the 403 was a 404-shaped answer about the path and not a statement
about anonymity.

Re-run on 2026-10-22, three public packages:

```bash
curl -s "https://ghcr.io/token?scope=repository:catthehacker/ubuntu:pull&service=ghcr.io"
# 200, 69 bytes: a token JSON body
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Accept: application/vnd.oci.image.index.v1+json" \
  "https://ghcr.io/v2/catthehacker/ubuntu/manifests/act-latest"
# 200, 754 bytes, schemaVersion 2, application/vnd.oci.image.index.v1+json
```

`actions/actions-runner` returned 200 with a 73-byte token and a 1,609-byte manifest.
`homebrew/core/hello` returned 200 with a 69-byte token and a 9,610-byte manifest at tag `2.12.3`.
The control, `library/hello-world`, returned 403 with 86 bytes every time, which is why the error
was invisible: the writer's own control was the thing under test and it was the wrong resource.

Digests of the saved responses, so the next session can check this claim rather than trust it:
token `e26b35c1dc64bf51b6e02f5a20f7d7fbf436a944d445155e8fc313a42ec3a808`, manifest
`62d572b92f9f32d3427b6d220ad1f9dca9c7b6ffad37d295425037dbff78abaf`.

## What we believed

`Cloudflare Email Routing for inbound -> Brevo for 300 a day out` was presented as a
working chain: "a whole inbound and outbound mail presence on one domain for the
price of the domain". Nothing in `docs/email/` mentioned SPF, DKIM or MX. `grep -rn "SPF\|DKIM\|MX record" docs/email/` returned no line.

## What we found

Three things, and the second is the one that changes the advice.

**The collision is at DMARC and not at SPF.** Brevo's authentication article states:
"The SPF and MX records are not required to authenticate a domain. We only provide
these records when setting up a dedicated IP." On the free shared-IP tier Brevo
writes a Brevo code TXT, a DKIM record and a DMARC record. Cloudflare writes MX, one
SPF record and a DKIM record at its own selector. Two DKIM selectors coexist, and
only one provider wrote an SPF record, so the two halves do not fight over it. What they do share is `_dmarc`, where one record may exist. Brevo's flow asks before
replacing an existing DMARC record, so the collision is a decision rather than a
silent overwrite.

**On a dedicated IP the collision is real and the merge is mandatory.** Brevo then
provides SPF and MX, and a domain may carry only one SPF record. Brevo publishes
a merge article for this case.

**The chain works on one domain, with a caveat about alignment.** Without a branded
subdomain "SPF passes via Brevo's infrastructure, not your own domain", so on the
shared tier SPF alignment rests on Brevo's return-path and DMARC passes on DKIM
alignment. A reader who wants strict SPF alignment adds a `mail.` subdomain.
supersedes: `docs/email/free/inbound.md` §The complete pair, in its previous form, which called the chain "the single most useful chain in the topic" without stating what its two halves do to one zone's DNS
title: The Cloudflare-plus-Brevo chain was claimed and never run, and its two halves meet at DMARC

**What was claimed.** That Cloudflare's egress pool spans three ASN numbers and a
draw lands in one at random, so a rung-4 block is intermittent rather than total. That was the corrected form of an earlier and worse claim that the transport
selected the ASN.

**What sharpens it.** A 24-draw run on 2026-10-24 returned **9 distinct IPv4
addresses, all AS13335**:

```
104.28.153.126  104.28.163.81  104.28.166.120  104.28.166.126  172.69.58.194
172.70.127.93   172.70.130.177 172.70.179.42   172.71.254.78     all AS13335
```

In a 30-draw set the AS14789 address `172.69.76.180` appeared once. So the IPv4
pool is roughly **97% AS13335**, and "three ASNs at random" overstated the spread
by implying a third of draws would land elsewhere.

**What is genuinely deterministic.** The IPv6 `fetch()` path returns
`2a06:98c0:3600::103` on every request, and RIPE puts that in
`2a06:98c0:3600::/48` → **AS132892 CLOUDFLARE**. Five consecutive reads returned
the same address. That is a fixed address in a different ASN number, reachable by
asking for a name with an AAAA record.

⭐ **So the honest form of the finding is this:** on IPv4 you cannot choose the ASN,
and you will almost always get AS13335. On IPv6 you get a different ASN every time,
by construction. If an upstream counts ASN numbers, the IPv6 road answers and the
IPv4 road does not. If it counts the organisation, neither helps, because all three
holders read "Cloudflare, Inc."

**Where the correction lives.** `docs/ip-proxy/README.md` §1 and
`docs/ip-proxy/techniques.md` §1. Neither has been observed.
title: The IPv6 road is deterministic; the IPv4 pool is not

body:
**What was claimed.** That Cloudflare's transports each exit from a different ASN,
so switching transport was a free lever against a gate counting ASNs. The evidence
was one address per transport:

| transport | one draw | ASN |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `fetch()` | `172.69.76.180` | AS14789 |
| raw `connect()` | `104.28.155.104` | AS13335 |
| IPv6 `fetch()` | `2a06:98c0:3600::103` | AS132892 |

**What took it away.** A paired 6-draw test on 2026-10-24, from one vantage point,
alternating the two transports:

```text
fetch()    172.71.254.79   172.70.127.94   104.28.166.120   all AS13335
sockets    104.28.163.81   104.28.153.140  104.28.162.236   all AS13335
```

`fetch()` returned `104.28.166.120`, which `cf-sockets` also returned in the same
run. The two transports draw from **one pool**. RIPE resolves every one of the
twelve addresses above to AS13335. In a 30-draw set the AS14789 address appeared
once, from plain `fetch()`. So the ASN is a property of the `/24` the pool happened to hand out, not of the
transport. That makes a rung-4 block more likely to be intermittent than total. It is not a
lever, and the rung-4 experiment is still unrun.

**Where the correction lives.** `docs/ip-proxy/README.md` §1 and
`docs/ip-proxy/techniques.md` §1 both carry the refutation and the reproduce
command. The 12 paired draws here
show the opposite, with overlapping addresses.
title: The transport does not select the ASN

**What was claimed.** The correction earlier on 2026-10-26 ranked six vendors. It
put Layer7 first at EUR 9.06 a month or EUR 86.97 a year, Rabisu second at
USD 10.99 a month or USD 8.79 annual with "a vendor FAQ that claims a genuine
licence", then NetVolo, HOSTKEY, Linveo and netcup. The segments were the offer archives,
US budget hosts, Russia and the CIS, Europe, the Windows specialists, the RDP
resellers, Turkey and MENA, Asia-Pacific, rented dedicated servers, the
hyperscalers, hosted desktops, WHMCS and wholesale resellers, the price
aggregators, the install and policy checks, the licence channel, and a cart audit. The Windows-specialist merge alone ranks
58 rows that clear 16 GiB, 4 vCPU and 50 GB. The first two passes had covered 11
vendors and then 6.

**What held.** The floor did not move. Layer7 is still the cheapest machine at
EUR 9.06 a month, which is USD 10.14, for 4 cores, 16 GiB and 80 GB with a
Windows Server 2019 or 2022 evaluation image on the OS list. The rendered
configurator closes at 4.90 + 1.92 + 2.24 = 9.06. The annual figure is 86.97, from
47.04 + 18.43 + 21.50, and it is arithmetic on three printed annual components
rather than a rendered total, so it stays `inferred`. No page prints a VAT line,
so whether 9.06 is net or gross is still unstated. The first payment on the annual
term is USD 97.48 at 1.1209 USD/EUR, the rate read on 2026-10-26; at the table's
1.1193 it is USD 97.34.

**What changed.** Three claims moved and one number was added. 1. **Rabisu's licence is unresolved.** The configurator prices Windows Server
   2012R2, 2019 and 2022 at no surcharge, and the monthly cycle is the default. But no licence sentence appears on the configurator, on the home page or in the
   knowledgebase: "licen", "Licen", "genuine" and "license" all return zero matches
   on 127,944, 133,582 and 94,572 bytes. The quote the earlier entry relied on did
   not reproduce. A zero surcharge is evidence of a price, not of a licence, so the
   row is now the cheapest with a Windows image and no claim about the licence. 2. **HostBrr is out of the ranking.** One merge ranked its Value 16GB third at
   USD 11.00 for 4 cores, 16 GiB and 160 GB on the strength of page prose and a
   logo tile. The order page is a registration wall that reaches a different
   product group, prints a zero subtotal, and offers no OS selector before payment. The page states no IPv4 either. 3. **VDSina is priced per day, not per month.** USD 4.08 is a daily rate, said
   three ways on the page and in its own plan JSON. At 30 days it is about
   USD 122.40 a month, so the row leaves any monthly ranking. 4. **The licence has a number.** Windows Server Standard is USD 509.99 one-off for
   16 core licences, which is USD 14.17 a month over 36 months, against Microsoft's
   USD 1,176 suggested MSRP for the 2025 edition. Datacenter is USD 2,499.99, or
   USD 69.44 a month. Sixteen cores is a per-server minimum, so a 4 vCPU machine
   pays the same licence as a 16 core one.

**What else the sweep settled.** Three hosts cannot install Windows at all, on the
vendor's own words: DigitalOcean, Linode/Akamai and Hostinger. OVHcloud VPS runs
Windows only if it was selected at order time. Seven rows joined the ranking and
netcup left it: Virtarix at USD 27.40, where the licence is printed as a USD 16.00
OS template inside the price and the Linux twin at USD 11.40 makes the decomposition
exact; windowsvps.host at USD 36.00 with a Datacenter licence claimed included; ServerPacket at USD 32.19, with the vendor's own pages 2.3 times apart for the same
shape; Kimsufi KS-3 at USD 64.00 all-in, which prints the licence as its own
USD 34.00 line on a USD 30.00 box; By-Hoster at USD 19.04, which states plainly that
it neither supplies nor resells a licence; Saganetwork at USD 8.23 ex VAT and
USD 9.88 paid, the cheapest row a buyer can start monthly, with its Windows path
unverified because the cart has no OS field; and InterServer at USD 40.00, which is
no longer the floor and is now one row among these.

**What is true now.** The cheapest machine that boots Windows at 16 GiB, 4 vCPU and
50 GB is Layer7 at EUR 9.06 a month (USD 10.14) or EUR 86.97 a year (USD 8.11 a
month). The cheapest startable monthly is Saganetwork at USD 8.23 ex VAT. The
cheapest with a Windows image at no surcharge is Rabisu at USD 10.99 monthly or
USD 8.79 annual, with the licence unresolved. The cheapest with the licence printed
is Virtarix at USD 27.40. No machine was booted and no order was placed.

**Where the correction lives.** `docs/compute/paid/windows-vps.md` owns the
ranking. A Rabisu renewal that charges for the licence would remove the
leading licence row and leave Layer7 as the answer, but it would not move the
floor. A ServerPacket order screen that prices the shape at USD 167.88 a year would
put it fifth at about USD 13.99. A Contabo Windows add-on price would put a 24 GiB
machine at the EUR 14.00 machine rate into the table, and no row up to Virtarix
offers more than 16 GiB.

**What a future session should do differently.** Two lessons. Re-read the sentence on the vendor's own page before it becomes a
ranking input. And a JSON-LD block is not a price: HOSTKEY's ruble card carries
`"priceCurrency":"EUR"` beside a RUB 3,390 figure, which is how a ruble machine can
be read as a euro one, and the EUR 14.00 the corpus records for it sits on a
storefront that answers 403.

Earlier waves show the cost: 4% to 13% of slugs in a wave were written
by two or more lanes, nine of twelve wave-landing commits needed a repair commit within an hour, and one compute
day produced 68 lane reports, about 569 KB, for one parent to read.

## What we found

A run now has one writer. Lanes propose changes with a capture of the page and an exact quote; `scripts/rq
integrate` applies them on a run branch with compare-and-set on the old value, the rung order, dedupe, the schema
and the record rules, and writes a ledger line with the old value. A second model re-reads a sample of each
unit's claims from the captures. A unit above the threshold is undone from its ledger and queued again. A run
lands as a pull request, and only when no gate check fails that passed on main. Four runs went through it on 2026-10-28:

| run | units of work | new records | claims audited | unsupported | units undone | pull request |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| verify compute (stale and inherited records) | 4 | 0 | 94 | 10 (10.6%) | 2 | #5 |
| expand compute (eleven LowEndTalk vendors) | 5 | 11 | 28 | 1 (3.6%) | 0 | #7 |
| verify compute (the two undone units, again) | 2 | 0 | 56 | 4 (7.1%) | 1 | #14 |
| expand inference (no-card rate limits) | 20 | 44 | 289 | 14 (4.8%) | 3 | #15 |

Over the four runs, 467 claims were re-read by a second model and 29 were unsupported (6.2%). The fourth run was
started by a parent agent given one line and nothing else: "Expand inference free LLM inference APIs that answer
without a card, with their rate limits". The runs also found ten defects in the harness itself, all fixed in #6 and #9:

1. Lint did not run the record rules, so a lane that set fields without a `confirm` (rule C10) or wrote
   narrative into a draft field (C20) learned it only from a rejection at integration. 2. Lint and briefs read records from the main checkout, so a reconcile unit on a record added earlier in the
   same run was refused. 3. Dedupe treated any shared deep URL as the same offer. A forum list page cited by four vendors merged three of
   them into the fourth. A shared page now counts only on the vendor's own domain. 4. The audit planner walked paths with a split on dots and missed list indexes, so claims read `null`. 5. The audit planner paired each claim about a new record with its first evidence row only. 6. The audit planner audited values itself had marked `unverified`. 7. Unsupported claims of a unit that passed its audit went to a folder nothing read. They are conflicts now. 8. The Wilson bound was applied to audits that read every claim of a unit, where nothing is extrapolated, so one
   wrong claim in eleven undid four new records. A census audit now fails on the observed rate alone. 9. The undo did not remove list items a unit had appended. 10. A run that added `documented` records could not land, because no document cited them. `rq land` now merges
    the current main into the run branch and re-renders the generated tables before it compares the gate.

**Ctrl-C.club's signups are closed and the destination had dropped the fact.** The

reader walks into. It set `class: changed`,
`cost_usd: unknown` and an empty quote, and it wrote down what would recover the
row: a first-party page that names an operator and a signup path. Its own
`free_tier.stated` conceded "no quota, lifetime or login policy was published to
either pass" and its `limits_note` said "the terms are unread", which is a record
arguing against its own verdict on one screen.

sentence in `identity_cost.detail`, the soft-limit wording in `notes`, and two
`evidence` entries from `signup.ctrl-c.club/`. The document row now reads "email,

**tilde.zone** is `confidence: unverified` with `verdict: qualifies-with-caveat`,
which is the honest pair: the reachability is measured and the offer is not
established. The record says in its own `notes` that recovering it needs what R22

its verdict field what its confidence field says. `qualifies-with-caveat` is the

rung is where the doubt is recorded. That is a schema limitation and not this
record's finding.

evidence. The general lesson is the one this repository keeps relearning. A correction that
lives in a seed's review file does not survive a rewrite unless the rewrite reads
the review file.
